title: AI for Code Optimization
abstract: We build frameworks that turn GPU performance diagnostics into code changes that a large language model (LLM) writes, compiles, and checks. Our OPTIMAS framework produced correct code in all 3,410 experiments and a speedup in over 98.82% of them on an NVIDIA H100. We release every prompt, response, and runtime measurement as an open dataset.

title: AI for HPC Decision Making
abstract: We build decision-support systems that tell HPC users and schedulers how to configure a job, how to change a past run, and what will happen if a parameter changes. Each suggestion comes with the evidence behind it and a trust label. In a scheduler simulator on production traces, COMPASS cut average job turnaround time by 25.53% and allocated 67.77% fewer nodes than ModelX, a state-of-the-art ML-based scheduler.

title: Few-Shot Transfer Learning for Performance
abstract: Few-shot transfer learning and generative AI significantly enhance the prediction of relative performance in HPC environments. By using a few samples from the target application, few-shot learning adapts the source model to improve generalizability, while generative AI synthesizes performance samples to mitigate data scarcity, ensuring accurate and efficient knowledge transfer across different platforms.

title: Representation Learning for Performance
abstract: We represent performance runs, anomalies, and source code as graphs and trees, so models learn from how samples relate to each other and not only from the features inside each one. Our PinG embeddings cut regression error by up to 61.67% on HPC data, and a graph model classified Chimbuko anomalies with 95% accuracy against 80% for XGBoost. When data is scarce, PerfGen synthesizes performance samples with generative AI.

title: Performance Characterization
abstract: Performance characterization is crucial as it identifies the key interactions between applications and hardware, captured by performance counters, which are essential for predicting execution times and guiding optimization efforts. It serves as a prerequisite to performance optimization and autotuning by providing insights into bottlenecks and resource usage patterns, allowing for informed adjustments that enhance overall system performance. Without this foundational understanding, tuning efforts are less effective and may not fully leverage the potential of HPC systems.

title: Performance Reproducibility
abstract: The same job, run twice with the same configuration on the same system, can take different amounts of time because of network traffic, power limits, task placement, and other jobs. We measure which settings drive this run-to-run variation, record the provenance and performance metadata needed to explain it in workflows, and find its causes inside large GPU traces. On a production cluster, our analysis cut the number of configurations a user must test to get fast and repeatable runs by up to 97%.

title: HPC+Edge Scheduling
abstract: We schedule deep learning inference across the CPU and integrated GPU on a single edge node, so neither device sits idle. Our schedulers improved inference performance by 1.5% to 48.1% over single-device and even-split baselines, and our 2025 ILP-based rate monotonic scheduler received the Best Paper Award at IEEE Cloud Summit. Our latest scheduler builds schedules offline and cuts runtime scheduling overhead by about 28x.

title: Applications
abstract: The methods we build for performance data also apply to health care and biology, where labeled data is scarce. We have predicted stress onset in autistic college students from wearable data, personalized fall-detection models with ModelXc, and predicted the effect of protein mutation pairs from a quarter of the possible mutants. Our stress models reached 69% accuracy for autistic students and 72% for neurotypical students.

title: Tools and Systems
abstract: We build the software that connects scientists to large systems: metadata stores for burst buffers, batch submission gateways, in-situ anomaly detection, and hardware simulators. MetaKV sped up metadata put and get operations by up to 2.66x and 6.29x over state-of-the-art key-value stores.

title: Education
abstract: We train students to build HPC software that scales, including parallel I/O, which most curricula leave out. HPC@SCALE is our hands-on course at Texas State, and we help set community priorities for the scientific computing workforce through the NGE workshop series.

title: CESAR Co-Design: Proxy Application Development and Validation
abstract: Proxy applications stand in for large production codes during hardware procurement and co-design, but whether a proxy behaves like its parent was usually judged by the developer's intuition. We built a machine-learning method that measures, per hardware resource, how much of the parent's performance behavior a proxy covers. Applied to XSBench, RSBench, and CMT-Bone, it shows which resources each proxy covers and which ones it misses.

title: MPI and MPI_T
abstract: In the past I have contributed to designing fault-tolerant interface for MPI. I developed performance measurement tools for assessing the performance of MPI_T interface.

title: Performance under Power and Resilience
abstract: Large simulations lose work when machines fail and lose speed when power is capped. We built checkpointing systems that make saving and restoring state cheap enough to do often, on shared Condor grids and on supercomputers, and algorithms that move unused power from jobs writing I/O to jobs computing. McrEngine cut checkpoint overhead by up to 87%, and I/O-aware power shifting sped up a high-priority job by up to 32%.

title: Cache Bottleneck Characterization
abstract: In this project, I built a robust low-level library for Intel's PEBS counter collection in user space, and developed an analysis approach for correlating PEBS data with application-specific information such as line number to characterize cache-access bottlenecks of applications.
